solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Public barney about leader of House — oust the government?

indicators.note: one word sits about, that is around, another, so the row wraps the selected letter

parts.note: public means open, not hidden

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, so only the start of the next word is kept

parts.note: the first letter of House
a barney is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A noisy public row breaks out around the Commons Speaker as rebels try to topple the government.
explanation.walkthrough: A barney is British slang for a quarrel. The row goes about H, after OVERT.
explanation.definitionFit: To overthrow is to remove a ruler or regime by force, which is exactly ousting a government.

clue.text: From a biblical book: "Thus, it came to pass, were the News of the Screws hacks"

definitions.text: Thus, it came to pass, were the News of the Screws hacks

parts.note: from in the sense of out of a place
taken as written
the Book of Job in the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A mock-scriptural verse records the fate of the reporters when Murdoch closed his scandal-hit Sunday paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The News of the World, nicknamed the News of the Screws, was shut in 2011 after the phone-hacking scandal, and its journalists lost their posts.
explanation.definitionFit: When the paper closed, its hacks (journalists) found themselves unemployed, which is what this phrase means.

clue.text: Vibrating part of organ's murder if stimulated without one

indicators.note: stimulated letters are stirred up and moved about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
one is A; without is used in its old sense of outside, so it is added on alongside

explanation.surface: Musical mischief: a church organ's vibrating part might commit murder if overexcited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests the instrument, but it is the ear. 'Without' here means outside, an old sense, bringing the extra A into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The eardrum is the membrane in the ear that vibrates in response to sound waves.

clue.text: (& 17dn.) Rupert's tabloid replacement making thousands (funny!) "accepting end of sleaze" — F-off!

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece is taken inside the others
making means building something new out of materials, so the letters are reworked
read literally as F off, telling us to remove that letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before its F is removed

indicators.note: 'end of' keeps only the last letter of 'sleaze'

parts.note: the final letter of sleaze

explanation.surface: Murdoch's new Sunday tabloid is mocked as a money-spinner built on sleaze, with a rude dismissal at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: FUNNY loses its F to leave UNNY; with THOUSANDS and the E of sleaze, all fourteen letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Murdoch launched this Sunday edition of his daily paper in 2012 to replace the closed News of the World.

clue.text: Right old set-to when draft put before Commons

indicators.note: placing one item before another sets them side by side in that order

parts.note: a rough is a first draft or sketch
the House of Commons

explanation.surface: A fine old row breaks out when a draft bill is laid before the Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' here is the British intensifier, as in a right mess, not the direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough-house is a boisterous brawl or disorderly fight, a proper set-to.

clue.text: Footballers' mates? Clowns

definitions.meaning: first meaning: acronym for wives and girlfriends of footballers

explanation.walkthrough: The tabloid label for England footballers' wives and girlfriends became famous at the 2006 World Cup.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the press acronym for players' partners and an old noun for humorous, joking people.

clue.text: Blair at last is in dirty film: 'Pushy Bunch'

indicators.note: something that is in another sits inside it

parts.note: scum is a dirty film on a liquid

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the name before it

parts.note: the last letter of Blair

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, it is claimed, appears in a sleazy film whose title is a jokey name for a gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests a movie but means a thin layer. A rugby scrum is a bunch of players pushing against each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrum is a tight pack of rugby forwards shoving, or any jostling crowd, so a pushy bunch.

clue.text: Pathetic Salmond gutted with uninitiated Act, revealing his origins

indicators.note: pathetic suggests something feeble and in a poor state, so the letters are jumbled
gutting removes the insides, so the middle letter goes
without its initial, the first letter is dropped

parts.note: the name as written, before its middle is removed
taken as written, before its first letter goes

explanation.surface: A satirical jab at Alex Salmond, gutted by some legislation, his roots laid bare.
explanation.walkthrough: Salmond loses his middle M to give SALOND, and Act loses its A to give CT. Alex Salmond was then First Minister of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Alex Salmond was born in Linlithgow, so his origins lie in that country, which he led.

clue.text: Maroon nuts: very royal family!

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
v is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A cry of delight at some maroon-coloured nuts fit for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like a colour or a castaway, but it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanovs were the dynasty that ruled Russia until the 1917 revolution.

clue.text: Miliband into microphone: "Quack"

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside

parts.note: mic is short for microphone
Ed Miliband, then Labour leader

explanation.surface: The Labour leader speaks into a microphone and all that comes out is a duck noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quack' sounds like the duck's call but is slang for a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Quack is informal slang for a doctor, and a medic is likewise a doctor or medical worker.

clue.text: Blunt set out to trap Brenda

indicators.note: trapping something means closing around it
out suggests something disordered or put out of place, so the letters move

parts.note: taken as written
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A spy-story feel: Anthony Blunt sets out to ensnare the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunt' looks like Anthony Blunt, the Queen's art adviser exposed as a Soviet spy, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Blunt speech is short and to the point, just as terse speech is curt and brief.

clue.text: Go round 'em, dithering, Boris Johnson-fashion?

indicators.note: dithering is dashing indecisively this way and that, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written, with 'em as EM

explanation.surface: A dithering mayor tries to dodge the issue, much like Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris Johnson, then Mayor of London, was famous for his tousled, uncombed hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's trademark untidy mop of hair makes him the very model of an unkempt look.

clue.text: Shy, antisocial four, each pissed

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Four unsociable people, each one drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is borrowed from French and describes a sullen, wild shyness.
explanation.definitionFit: Farouche describes someone sullenly shy and unsociable in company, from the French for wild.

clue.text: Old president losing weight with chip surgery

indicators.note: a word that loses something has those letters taken away

parts.note: Bill Clinton, former US president
a ton is a unit of weight
IC, integrated circuit, is a microchip

explanation.surface: A former president slims down and has a microchip implanted in an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surgery' suggests an operation, but in Britain a surgery is also a doctor's consulting room.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a surgery is a place where patients see a doctor, much like a medical centre.

clue.text: Labour party's constitution, once stoical, is slapdash and small

indicators.note: slapdash means carelessly thrown together, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
s is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A dig at New Labour: the party's once-steady founding principles have become sloppy and shrunken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitution' suggests a rulebook, but here it means what the party was made up of.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour was once composed of left-wingers committed to public ownership, so its makeup was those people.

clue.text: Pause in talking to penetrate law enforcer (screw)

indicators.note: penetrating something means getting inside it

parts.note: a JP, Justice of the Peace, is a magistrate
um is the sound of a hesitation in speech

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a hesitant speaker and a prison officer, screw being slang for a warder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' looks like the prison warder that law enforcer hints at; it is slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are vulgar slang verbs for having sex with someone.

clue.text: Clinton's ultimate painful ejaculation, nothing right, nerve broken, no second chance

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the last one of the name

parts.note: the last letter of Clinton

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart and reassembled in a different order

parts.note: ow is a cry of pain
zero, nothing
r is the abbreviation for right
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A smutty Clinton-Lewinsky scene: a painful climax, losing his nerve, with no second go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ejaculation' is used in its old sense of a sudden exclamation, not the sexual one the surface pushes.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is now or never means the opportunity must be taken immediately or will be lost.

clue.text: Cane that's grown to be a vulgar retaliatory response

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fruit bush grown on canes in the garden
second meaning: a rude noise made with the tongue and lips, a Bronx cheer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cane' suggests corporal punishment, setting up a revenge story, but it is a garden plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit grows on tall canes, and blowing one is the rude spluttering noise of derision.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Knockabout slip on this fruity thing?

definitions.text: Knockabout slip on this fruity thing?

parts.words: Knockabout slip on this fruity thing?
parts.note: surface reading: a slapstick tumble on the peel of a fruit
setter's reading: the classic comic pratfall prop, and by extension any embarrassing political blunder

explanation.walkthrough: In British political journalism this phrase means a gaffe that trips a politician up, as well as the cartoon prop.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow peel is the archetypal slapstick cause of a fall, hence a byword for an embarrassing mistake.

clue.text: Not a thing to stick up groupie on trip

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means writing it bottom to top

parts.note: a groupie is an obsessive fan
a trip is a stumble or fall

explanation.surface: A groupie stumbles, and there is nothing to hold them upright.
explanation.walkthrough: Naff all is British slang for nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang phrase means nothing whatsoever, so not a thing.

clue.text: Shag, especially holding Times

indicators.note: the words hold the solution inside them, across the gap between them

parts.note: sitting across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A lewd remark about having sex, particularly while reading the Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper, a Murdoch paper, but means periods of history.
explanation.definitionFit: Ages are long periods or eras, as are times in the sense of historical epochs.

clue.text: Coward, maybe old con, tipped over vessel

indicators.note: a column that is tipped over ends up the other way round

parts.note: Noël Coward, the English playwright, is one example of a Noel
an old lag is a long-serving convict

explanation.surface: A playwright, or perhaps a former convict, capsizes a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward' reads as a timid person, but it is Noël Coward. 'Maybe' flags that he is one example of a Noël.
explanation.definitionFit: A galleon was a large sailing ship of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, a type of vessel.

clue.text: Black, relatively deprived America that's gone overboard

parts.note: jet black, the deepest black

indicators.note: deprived of a relative, so the family-member word is removed from the name

parts.note: Uncle Sam personifies the United States

explanation.surface: A comment on poverty among black Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relatively deprived' sounds like sociology but means the relative (UNCLE) is taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Jetsam is cargo thrown overboard from a ship, things that have gone over the side.

clue.text: Perpetrate doggy-style act on the street of blue rocks?

definitions.text: Perpetrate doggy-style act on the street

indicators.note: rocks means shakes about, so the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Mock-smutty: a doggy-style sex act in public, straight out of a blue movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doggy-style' pretends to be sexual; what dogs do on the street is foul the pavement.
explanation.definitionFit: To befoul is to make dirty, as a dog does when it fouls a pavement.

clue.text: Personal stink associated with Murdoch title, officer

parts.note: BO, body odour
the Sun, Rupert Murdoch's tabloid

explanation.surface: A Murdoch executive is accused of a personal whiff of scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Title' suggests a rank, fitting 'officer', but it is a newspaper title.
explanation.definitionFit: A bosun, or boatswain, is a ship's officer in charge of equipment and crew.

clue.text: Society with airs (bloody hell, admitting Labour leader) gets some stick

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: gee is a mild exclamation of surprise

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of Labour
a club is a heavy stick

explanation.surface: A snooty society swears when a Labour leader is let in and gets a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airs' suggests putting on airs, but means tunes; a glee is a part-song for unaccompanied voices.
explanation.definitionFit: A glee club is a choral society singing glees, short songs, so a society with tunes.

clue.text: Shrewd liar — no hesitation

indicators.note: with no hesitation, the speech-filler sound of a pause is removed

parts.note: Jeffrey Archer, the novelist and peer jailed for perjury
er is a hesitant sound

explanation.surface: A cunning liar who never pauses before spinning his story.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Archer, a Private Eye regular, was jailed in 2001 for perjury, hence the liar.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch means knowing and cunning, as in an arch look, so shrewd in a sly way.

clue.text: Tries to get elected, admitting "right swamped with publicity" — flags

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the outer word takes the rest inside

parts.note: to stand is to run for office

indicators.note: something swamped is engulfed, surrounded on all sides

parts.note: an ad, advertising
r is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A right-wing candidate gains a big publicity boost while running for office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flags' looks like a verb meaning tires, but it is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Standards are banners or flags carried as emblems, as in a regimental standard.

clue.text: Streak of sadomasochism? Attention!

parts.note: S and M, the abbreviation for sadomasochism
to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: A kinky streak is revealed, with a cry for everyone to listen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Streak' suggests a character trait, as in a streak of cruelty, but means a mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A smear is a streaky mark of something wiped on a surface.

clue.text: Kinnock: one abandoned, unprofessional, gutless dope

indicators.note: something abandoned is left behind, so it drops out of the name

parts.note: Neil Kinnock, former Labour leader
the Roman numeral for one, the letter to drop

indicators.note: without guts, the middle letter is taken out

parts.note: lay means not professional, as in a layman

explanation.surface: A cruel verdict on Neil Kinnock: a deserted, amateurish, spineless idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a nelly is a silly or foolish person, as in 'not on your nelly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dope is a stupid person, and nelly is British slang for a fool or weakling.

clue.text: Yes, ho-hum, twittering about Brown's end — here's a means of shutting up the blabber-mouth

definitions.text: a means of shutting up the blabber-mouth

indicators.note: about means around, so the other letters go around it
twittering is chattering nervously, so the letters flutter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a name is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of Brown

explanation.surface: Gossip on Twitter about Gordon Brown's downfall, and a bribe to silence a loose-tongued insider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twittering' hints at the social network, apt for a blabber-mouth, but it is just the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hush money is a bribe paid to keep someone from revealing secrets.
